title: Corey Haines' copywriting playbook: diagnose first, then write specific, supportable copy with no AI tells
summary: Corey's open-source copywriting skill for AI agents. It teaches diagnosing the input before drafting (blank brief, real voice, or point edit), locking copy unit by unit, and running every line through a three-question gate. It also bans AI tells and requires claims to be supportable.

principles.text: Diagnose the input before writing: blank brief, real voice present, or a point edit decides how much you may change.
principles.quote: Most bad AI copy comes from imposing the model's taste on a marketer who already made good choices, so the diagnosis sets how much you're allowed to change.

principles.text: Treat the writer's draft as evidence of taste: keep their vocabulary, emphasis, scope and angle rather than replacing them with yours.
principles.quote: Vocabulary is a voice choice. If they write "stuff" and "ship," don't upgrade to "solutions" and "deploy."

principles.text: Run every line through three questions: can the reader picture it, can it be proven true or false, and could a competitor write it?
principles.quote: Could a competitor write this exact sentence? If yes, it fails (the swap test).

principles.text: Write only claims the source material supports. When declining a claim, name the evidence that would unlock it.
principles.quote: A declined claim with an unlock path is an action item for the client; without one it's a dead end.

principles.text: Choose clarity over cleverness; clearer positioning is tied to better conversion, shorter sales cycles and lower CAC.
principles.quote: If you have to choose between clear and creative, choose clear.

principles.text: Ration the punch: keep most lines plain and specific, with only one or two punchy moments per page.
principles.quote: When every line is trying to land, none do, and the stacked devices read as AI.
